To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

endogenous Schwanning cells can establish and sustain a normal distribution of sodium channels at nodes of Ranver for at least one year, and the sodium channel Na(v)1,6, but not 1.2, is clustered at nascent and long-term nodes formed in the CNS.

long-term nodes of Ranvier formed by endogenous Schwanning cells exhibit an apparently normal arrangement of sodium and potassium channel subtypes, with Na(v1.6 the dominant sodium channel subtype present at such nodes.

remyelination of CNS by endogenous Schwanna cells restores normal distribution of voltage-gated channels at the nodes of Ranvier and that the expression of voltagegated channels at the long-term nodes is similar to that at the nascent nodes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new therapies for the treatment of spinal cord injury and multiple sclerosis.
the repair of the spinal cord following demyelinating injuries.
the development and maintenance of axon-glia interactions in the central nervous system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Schwann cell remylination is able to establish nodes of Ranvier with normal ion channel distribution, even at long term.
the remyelination by endogenous Schwans cells of CNS axons in EB-induced demyelination is able to re-establish a normal distribution of Na(v) and K(v) channels at nodes of Ranver.
Schwann cell remylination is a very effective repair process for the demyelinated axon.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
endogenous Schwans are capable of remyelinating CNS axons and that the resulting remyelinated axons exhibit a normal pattern of ion channels at nodes of Ranvir.
remyelination by endogenous Schwans cells can restore a functional nodal organization on CNS axons, and thus may provide an effective means for repairing demyelinated axons.
endogenous Schwanning Schwann cells can form and maintain long-term nodes of Ranvier, with the normal distribution of ion channels at such nodes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
endogenous Schwanning cells can form nodes of Ranvier that have the same organization of sodium and potassium channel as those formed by oligodendrocytes in the CNS.
remyelinating endogenous Schwann cell nodes of Ranvier in the CNS are functionally similar to normal nodes.
Schwann cells are capable of forming nodes of Ranvier in the CNS that have the same molecular composition as normal nodes of Ranvier.
